references.text: God commands Israel to be holy because He is holy. This theme of holiness as a requirement for God's people is directly linked to the command to be 'holy people' in Exodus 22:30.
God's command, 'You shall be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy,' parallels the requirement to be 'holy people' in the main verse.
Addresses the prohibition against eating animals that died naturally or were torn apart, expanding on the rule not to eat meat from beasts torn to pieces in the field.
Repeats the prohibition against eating meat from animals killed by tearing and emphasizes the requirement of holiness for the priests.
Forbids eating animals that died naturally because Israel is a holy people to the Lord, noting that such meat may be given to foreigners or sold.
Ezekiel declares that he has never eaten an animal that died naturally or was torn apart, showing how this law was practiced by the righteous.
The priests shall not eat anything that died naturally or was torn apart, whether of birds or animals. This confirms the enduring prohibition from Exodus.
Peter quotes Leviticus and applies the requirement of holiness to Christians: 'Be holy, for I am holy.' This shows the New Testament continuation of the call to holiness.
Christians are called 'a holy people' who belong to God, reflecting Exodus 22:30's requirement that God's people be holy men and women.
Both verses are built on the principle that life is holy and belongs to God, requiring abstention from meat where the blood has not been fully drained or where the animal died violently.
Genesis 9:4 establishes the universal principle (life = blood) which Exodus 22:30 later specifies and applies to Israel regarding meat from animals torn by predators.
Acts 15:29 continues and confirms the Mosaic law's prohibition against eating meat from strangled or torn animals in the new covenant.
